newsitem.title: USA: U.S. shuttle to fly satellite on robot arm.
newsitem.headline: U.S. shuttle to fly satellite on robot arm.

text.p: The five-member crew of the shuttle Columbia faced a second mission with a prototype space factory on Tuesday, one day after successfully retrieving it from orbit.

On Monday night, astronaut Tom Jones used Columbia's robot arm to snatch the Wake Shield Facility from its orbit around Earth after shuttle commander Ken Cockrell manoeuvred the orbiter around and beneath the free-floating satellite.
The operation was made more complicated by a second satellite also released from Columbia, the Orfeus-Spas telescope, travelling through space nearby.

Concern that Orfeus-Spas might draw too close to Wake Shield for a safe recovery had prompted NASA to move up by three hours the time of the retrieval. But everything went smoothly during the manuever as the two multi-million dollar satellite remained a safe distance apart, NASA officials said.

On Tuesday evening, beginning at 7:06 p.m. EST (0006 GMT on Wednesday), the 12-foot (4-meter) diameter Wake Shield was to sail through space attached to Columbia's 50-foot (17-meter) robotic arm until 10:41 p.m. EST (0341 GMT on Wednesday).

After that the astronauts were to draw in the satellite and stow it in the shuttle's cargo bay until the orbiter's landing, scheduled for Dec. 5 at 7:40 a.m. EST (1240 GMT) at the Kennedy Space Centre.

Wake Shield, a prototype "factory" that produces ultrapure material for use in semiconductors and other high-tech applications, was to make oxide chips from oxygen encountered during its trip on Tuesday night.
Columbia's crew was sleeping on Tuesday morning. They were due to be awakened at 2:56 p.m. EST (1956 GMT), marking the start of their eighth day in orbit.
The Orfeus-Spas continued to trail behind Columbia. The shuttle was scheduled to retrieve the satellite on Dec. 3.
